title: Barnacle

pages.text:
Juno woke with the shell whistle clutched in her hand, her heart hammering against her ribs. The attic room was dark, but the air felt different. It tasted like salt and old stone. She swung her legs over the side of the bed, her yellow raincoat still on from the night before. It was a weird thing to sleep in, but she hadn’t wanted to be unready.

Downstairs, the house was quiet. She tiptoed past the kitchen, where a single bulb flickered, and out the back door onto the porch. The mud was still there, thick and grey, but it looked... softer. Less angry. She stepped down into the silt. It squelched under her boots, a sound that usually made her stomach turn. Today, it sounded like a greeting.

She raised the spiral shell to her lips. She didn’t blow it. She just held it there, listening. The wind died. The gulls on the masts stopped their grumbling. The world held its breath.

"Honestly!"

The voice came from her left. Juno spun around, her puffs of curly dark-brown hair bouncing. There, sitting on a driftwood log in the grey muck, was a hermit crab. He was tiny, no bigger than a marble, and he wore a chipped blue teapot shell. He was waving one claw frantically.

"Don't gawk," the crab said, his voice high and reedy. "It’s undignified."
pages.image: Juno in her yellow raincoat standing in grey harbor mud, looking shocked at a tiny hermit crab in a blue teapot shell sitting on a log.

pages.text:
Juno blinked. She looked at the crab. She looked at the empty air. She looked at the crab again.

"Did you... did you just talk?" she whispered.

"I am Barnacle," the crab said, straightening his teapot shell with a piece of kelp. "And yes. I talked. It is a very common occurrence, although I suspect you are not used to it. Most humans just see a bug and stomp. I prefer conversation."

Juno took a shaky step back. Her mind was racing. *Sea creatures. Only the Keeper hears them.* Grandma Ivy’s note flashed in her memory. *When the whistle is blown by someone listening, the sea will answer.*

"You’re a crab," Juno said, her voice trembling.

"I am a hermit crab," Barnacle corrected, offended. "And I was formerly the Royal Consultant to the Deep Court, or at least I was until the whole... catastrophe. Which you seem to have caused, or at least, failed to prevent."

Juno frowned. "I didn’t do anything. The tide stopped a year ago. Before I got here."

Barnacle sighed, a sound like a deflating balloon. "Oh, you sweet, stubborn child. You think you are the first to arrive? The tide stopped when the last Keeper died. No one has wound the Clock since. The sea is not gone, Miss Vale. It is sleeping. And it is getting very, very grumpy."
pages.image: A close-up of Barnacle, a grumpy hermit crab in a chipped blue teapot, gesturing with a claw while Juno looks on with wide eyes.

pages.text:
Juno sat down in the mud, not caring about her boots. The dampness soaked through her jeans, but she didn’t notice. Her brain was trying to make sense of the impossible. A talking crab. A sleeping sea. A magic shell.

"Grandma Ivy," she said softly. "She was a Keeper."

Barnacle’s eyes widened. He looked up at the sky, as if checking for spies. "She was the best. Elegant. Precise. She knew how to handle the Moon Gear. She knew how to sooth the Salt Compass. And you?" He looked Juno up and down. "You are wearing a raincoat in the morning. It is a lovely coat, but it is not a tide-keeper’s garment."

Juno hugged her knees. "I’m not brave, Barnacle. I’m just loud. And I’m new. I don’t even know how to open the front door without getting stuck in the hinges."

Barnacle hopped off the log. He walked over to Juno, his tiny legs clicking on the driftwood. He stopped right at her boot.

"Bravery is not about being silent," he said, his voice losing some of its bite. "It is about showing up. You showed up. You listened. The sea remembers that. That is why it answered you, and not the Mayor, or the Mayor’s dog, or that man in the silver car who parks his car in the mud."

Juno looked at the crab. "What do I do?"

"You wind the Clock," Barnacle said. "At the Grand Low. In nine days."
pages.image: Juno sitting in the mud, looking sad, while Barnacle stands on her boot, looking up at her with a serious expression.

pages.text:
"Nine days?" Juno’s stomach dropped. "Why does it have to be that specific night?"

Barnacle climbed up her leg, a sensation like a cold pebble moving up her sock. He climbed onto her shoulder and settled into the collar of her yellow raincoat. It was a strange feeling, but not unpleasant.

"The Tide Clock is not just a machine," Barnacle explained. "It is a heart. It beats with the moon. The Grand Low is the night the moon is highest and the pull is strongest. If the Clock is not wound then, the sea will forget this bay. It will forget the boats, the fish, the mud. It will become a dry hole in the earth. And I will be a very, very thirsty crab."

Juno rubbed her eyes. "That’s... that’s a lot of pressure for an eleven-year-old in a raincoat."

"It is a lot of pressure for anyone," Barnacle agreed. "But it is a very specific kind of pressure. You have to find the keys. Three of them. The Moon Pearl, the Salt Compass, and the Storm Bell. Your grandmother hid them. She was clever. She knew that if one person had them all, they could be stolen. So she split them up."

"Where?" Juno asked.

Barnacle shook his head. "She did not tell me. She told *her* log. The green one. The one you found in the attic."

Juno’s heart skipped a beat. The green cloth notebook with the brass clasp. She had read the first page. *When the whistle is blown by someone listening, the sea will answer.* But the rest? She hadn’t read the rest.
pages.image: Barnacle perched on Juno's shoulder, looking out over the grey harbor, with Juno’s yellow raincoat collar visible.

pages.text:
Juno climbed down from the log. Her legs were wobbly. The world felt bigger and more dangerous than it had that morning. But it also felt... alive. The mud was not just dirt. It was the skin of the ocean. And the ocean was waiting for her.

"I need to read the log," she said.

"Beg your pardon?" Barnacle said, adjusting his teapot shell.

"The log. Grandma Ivy’s log. It has to have the map. Or the clues. Or..." Juno trailed off. She didn’t know what else it could have. A recipe? A joke? A list of people who owed her money?

Barnacle looked at her with a mix of skepticism and something else. Hope, maybe. Or just a desire for the tide to return so he could stop feeling so dry.

"Go on, then," he said. "But hurry. The sun is coming up, and I have a reputation to maintain. I am not a crab who runs around in the daylight. It is simply bad for the shell."

Juno turned and ran back toward the house. Her boots squelched with every step. She didn’t look back. She couldn’t. If she looked back, she might see the mud swallowing the world, and she couldn’t afford to be afraid yet. She had a job to do. She had a sea to wake up. And she had exactly nine days to figure out how to do it.
pages.image: Juno running back toward the tall narrow house, her yellow raincoat bright against the grey morning, Barnacle invisible on her shoulder.

summary: Juno meets Barnacle, a talking hermit crab who reveals that the tide stopped because no one wound the Tide Clock after Grandma Ivy died. Barnacle explains that the sea is sleeping and will forget the bay if the Clock is not wound at the Grand Low in nine days. He tells Juno she must find three hidden keys, the Moon Pearl, the Salt Compass, and the Storm Bell, likely using clues in her grandmother's log.
